section.title: No Other Gospel
section.sectionRationale: The letter opens without the usual thanksgiving. Paul establishes his apostleship from Jesus Christ and God the Father, states the gospel in one line, that Christ gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, and then erupts in alarm that the Galatians are so quickly deserting the God who called them. This is the doorway to the whole letter: there is one gospel of grace, and any rival is no gospel at all.
section.thesis: There is only one true gospel, that Christ gave Himself for our sins to rescue us, and it comes from God and not from men; so any message that adds to it or replaces it is a desertion of God Himself and stands under His curse.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the greeting that grounds Paul's authority and the gospel in one sentence; the astonished rebuke that they are turning to a different gospel; and the double curse on any who preach another message, with Paul's refusal to court human approval.

units.label: Greeting and gospel in a sentence
units.note: an apostle from God, Christ who gave Himself

verses.text: Paul, an apostle, sent not from men nor by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead,
and all the brothers with me, To the churches of Galatia:
{{charis|Grace}} and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,
who gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father,
to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

units.label: Deserting the One who called you
units.note: amazed how quickly you are turning

verses.text: I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ and are turning to a different {{euangelion|gospel}},
which is not even a gospel. Evidently some people are troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ.

units.label: Let him be under a curse
units.note: the double anathema and Paul's aim to please God

verses.text: But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be {{anathema|under a curse}}!
As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be under a curse!
Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ.

charis.gloss: Grace, unmerited favor, the free gift of God. Paul's standard greeting is not empty courtesy; it announces the theme of the whole letter. The Galatians were called by the grace of Christ, verse 6, and the danger is that they trade that grace for a religion of law keeping. Grace is God giving what we could never earn.

euangelion.gloss: Gospel, good news, an announcement of victory. In the New Testament it is the news that God has acted in Christ to save sinners. Paul calls the rival message a different euangelion, then corrects himself: it is not even good news at all, because a gospel that rests on our works is no rescue. There is only one true gospel.

anathema.gloss: A thing devoted to destruction, accursed, given over to God's judgment. Paul pronounces this on anyone, even himself or an angel, who preaches a contrary gospel. The severity measures the stakes: to distort the gospel is not a minor error but an assault on the only message that saves.

basic.context: Paul writes to churches in Galatia that he had planted, and he is alarmed. Traveling teachers have arrived insisting that faith in Christ is not enough, that Gentile believers must also take on the law of Moses, starting with circumcision. Paul skips his usual words of thanks and goes straight to the point: there is one gospel, Christ gave Himself for our sins, and to add to it is to abandon it.
basic.hermeneutics: These opening verses set the tone and the theme. Paul defends where his authority comes from, states the gospel in a single sentence, and warns in the strongest terms against any rival. Read the rest of the letter in the light of this alarm: everything Paul argues flows from his conviction that the gospel of grace is being lost.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul greets them with charis, grace, the free favor of God that is the heartbeat of the letter. He is stunned they are turning to a different euangelion, a different gospel, then adds that it is no gospel at all. And he pronounces anathema, a curse, on anyone who preaches a contrary message, even an angel from heaven.
basic.typology: The rescue from the present evil age echoes the exodus, when God redeemed His people from slavery. Christ giving Himself for our sins fulfills the sacrificial system, where a substitute died in the place of the guilty. Paul's whole argument will show that these shadows find their reality in Christ, not in a return to the law.
basic.christ: The gospel is Christ Himself: He gave Himself for our sins to rescue us. His death is substitutionary, for our sins, and His resurrection is assumed in verse 1, God the Father who raised Him from the dead. To add anything to Christ is to say His self giving was not enough, which Paul will not allow.
basic.god: God is the Father who raised Jesus, the One who calls sinners by grace, and the One whose approval Paul seeks above all human opinion. God's will stands behind the rescue, verse 4, and His glory is the goal, verse 5. He is jealous for the purity of the gospel because it is the only way sinners are saved.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 1 says the gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. 1 Corinthians 15 gives the gospel in summary: Christ died for our sins and was raised. 2 Corinthians 11 warns of false apostles preaching another Jesus and another gospel.
basic.oneStory: From Eden onward the human problem is sin and the present evil age it has produced. Here in one line is God's answer: Christ gave Himself for our sins to rescue us. The whole Bible runs toward this rescue, and Paul will spend the letter guarding it against every counterfeit.

context.literary:
Galatians is a letter that breaks its own form. Ancient letters, and Paul's other letters, follow a recognisable order: sender, recipients, greeting, then a thanksgiving or blessing for the readers, then the business. Here the first three parts are present and are unusually full, but the thanksgiving never arrives. Verse 6 puts a 'I am amazed' exactly where the reader expects 'I thank my God.' The omission is the first piece of rhetoric in the letter and it does its work before Paul has said anything about circumcision.

The opening sentence, verses 1 to 5, is one long Greek sentence, and the greeting alone is swollen. The sender clause is expanded with a negation, 'not from men nor by man,' and a positive, 'by Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead.' The address is plain, 'the churches of Galatia,' with no word of praise that the other letters usually give. Then the greeting itself grows a relative clause that carries the whole gospel in one line, verse 4, and ends in a doxology, verse 5. The effect is that the greeting has already stated the thing the letter will defend.

The shift at verse 6 is abrupt. Verses 6 to 9 are tightly bound by repetition of the word 'gospel' and its cognate verb, five times in four verses, together with the repeated 'contrary to the one we preached' and the double curse. Verses 8 and 9 mirror one another: 'even if we or an angel from heaven' and 'if anyone,' 'we preached' and 'you received,' the same curse. The formula 'as we have said before, so now I say again' makes the second a deliberate echo, not carelessness.

Verse 10 is a hinge. It asks three questions in quick succession and ends on a conditional that becomes the opening thesis for the next section. By asking whether he is persuading men or God, Paul prepares for the long autobiography of 1:11 to 2:21, where the question of where the gospel came from is answered with a story.
context.historical:
Galatia could mean two things in Paul's day. In the north it was the old territory of Celtic settlers who had come into central Anatolia in the third century before Christ, around the cities of Ancyra, Pessinus and Tavium. By Paul's time the Romans had made it a province, and the province, formed in 25 BC, stretched far to the south and included Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, the cities of Paul's first journey in Acts 13 and 14. Which of the two Paul means by 'the churches of Galatia' has divided readers, and the question matters for dating the letter.

The churches were made up mostly of Gentiles who, as Paul says later, had once served beings that by nature are not gods, Galatians 4:8. They had received the gospel with remarkable warmth. Paul reminds them that they welcomed him in his illness 'as if I were an angel of God, as if I were Christ Jesus Himself,' Galatians 4:14. That makes the shift in verse 6 harder to bear and explains his astonishment.

The teachers who followed him told the converts that faith in Christ was not enough to make them part of Abraham's family. The sign of the covenant given to Abraham was circumcision, Genesis 17:9-14, and the command read 'every male... including those purchased from a foreigner.' Anyone reading Genesis 17 could see the logic. Their argument may also have tied the practice to the Jerusalem apostles. It would have been persuasive, since the Messiah was a Jew and the Scriptures were Jewish.

There was also a political edge. Within the Roman Empire, Jews had a recognised and tolerated place, while a new movement of uncircumcised Gentiles who worshipped the Jewish God might attract suspicion. Paul says at the end of the letter that those who press circumcision do so 'to avoid persecution for the cross of Christ,' Galatians 6:12. Alongside the theological appeal, there was pressure to look respectable.
context.canonical:
The opening verse takes up the biblical category of sending. Prophets were sent by God, as Isaiah heard, 'Whom shall I send?' Isaiah 6:8, and Jesus says to His disciples, 'As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you,' John 20:21. Paul draws on the same chain. He is an apostle, a sent one, and the one who sent him is the one who raised Jesus. The phrase 'who raised Him from the dead' is the first creedal note of the letter, and it joins Paul to the earliest summary of the gospel in 1 Corinthians 15:3-4.

The doxology and the language of rescue echo the Old Testament account of the exodus. The verb for rescue is the one the Greek Bible uses repeatedly of God delivering His people, and the 'present evil age' sets Christ's work in the framework of two ages, a pattern that runs through Daniel, the Gospels and Paul. The language of Colossians 1:13 is a close companion: 'He has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son.'

The warning against adding to a message has a long history. Moses forbids adding to or subtracting from the commands of God, Deuteronomy 4:2, and the book of Revelation closes with a similar warning, Revelation 22:18-19. The test of the true prophet in Deuteronomy 13:1-5 is whether he leads the people away from the Lord who redeemed them from slavery, even if he can do a sign. Paul's 'even if an angel from heaven' applies the same test to a more dazzling credential.

Other writers share the concern. Jude speaks of men who have crept in among the believers unnoticed, Jude 4, and Peter warns that false teachers will secretly introduce destructive heresies, 2 Peter 2:1. Paul himself uses the opening of Galatians as the template of the warning in 2 Corinthians 11:3-4, where a different Jesus and a different gospel are said to be accepted too easily.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wrote to bring a congregation back from the edge before the damage was done. He does not open with an argument about circumcision, and that is the first sign of his intent. He opens with Christ, with God, with the cross and with the will of the Father, so that the readers are reminded who it is they are turning from before they are told what they are turning to.

He meant the Galatians to understand that the choice before them was not between two versions of the same message. It was between the gospel and its absence. The statement in verse 7, that the other message is 'not even a gospel,' is meant to take away the middle ground. The teachers presented their message as a completion of what Paul had begun. Paul's reply is that something added as a condition is no addition at all but a replacement.

He also wanted the readers to see the cost. To go back to the law as a way of belonging to God's people was to desert 'the One who called you,' not merely to adjust a practice. Paul is not offended on his own behalf. The force of the curse in verses 8 and 9 is the force of someone defending a person he loves, as a parent might at the sight of a child walking toward a cliff.

Verse 10 shows his own motive and invites theirs. He is not trying to win a hearing by flattery, as the rival teachers might be. The closing question turns the letter toward a defence of his calling, because the Galatians need to know that what they received from him came from God and not from a human source that could be improved.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records Paul's greeting, his astonishment and his curse. It commands nothing in the form of an imperative, and yet it contains a strong teaching standard: the gospel already preached is the measure by which any later message is judged. 'The one you received' in verse 9 sets the rule that tradition does not outrank the apostolic message, and that no teacher, however impressive, is free to rewrite it.

The curse is a description of what happens to anyone who preaches a contrary gospel, and not a licence for ordinary believers to curse people they disagree with. Paul invokes God's judgment on a specific false teaching, and he does so at the cost of grief, as Romans 9:3 shows. Careful disagreement within the church over lesser matters is a different thing. Romans 14 gives room for that.

The passage also gives a pattern for applying the letter's test. Believers today are not asked to hunt for heresy under every difference of opinion. They are asked to know the gospel well enough to recognise a message that adds a requirement to the finished work of Christ. A modern version of the Galatian error may not involve circumcision at all, but may insist on some mark, practice or experience as a condition of full acceptance.

debates.question: Who were the churches of Galatia, and when was this letter written?

views.label: The northern region, ethnic Galatia
views.case: The older reading takes Paul to mean the territory of the Gauls, the area around Ancyra. It matches the plain sense of the word as ethnic, and Paul calls them 'foolish Galatians' in Galatians 3:1. On this view the letter was written later, after Paul's second journey, possibly from Ephesus.

views.label: The southern cities of the Roman province
views.case: The southern view says Paul would have used the Roman provincial name, as he does elsewhere for Asia and Macedonia. Acts 13 and 14 describe churches founded in those cities, and nothing in Acts speaks of a northern mission. This view allows a date soon after the first journey and lets Galatians 2 be read against Acts 11.

views.label: Left open
views.case: Some scholars decline to settle it because the letter's message does not depend on it, and the evidence is evenly balanced.

debates.bearing: The decision affects how the Jerusalem visits of chapter 2 are matched to Acts, but it does not alter the force of verses 1 to 10. The gospel defended is the same, and the readers are Gentile converts under pressure.

debates.question: Is the double curse a pronouncement of damnation or a warning?

views.label: A formal sentence of exclusion
views.case: The word anathema is the one the Greek Old Testament uses for what is devoted to destruction, as with Jericho in Joshua 6:17-18. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 16:22 of anyone who does not love the Lord. On this view it declares that the false teacher stands under God's judgment.

views.label: A solemn warning meant to bring repentance
views.case: Paul says 'let him be' under a curse, a wish more than a verdict, and he later hopes for the Galatians' recovery, Galatians 4:19-20. Elsewhere he is willing to be cursed for the sake of his people, Romans 9:3. The language is meant to shock readers into seeing what is at stake.

debates.bearing: The two views share the main point: the issue is serious enough for the strongest words in Paul's vocabulary. A message that adds conditions to the gospel puts people's salvation at risk, and love for them requires saying so plainly.

study.originalLanguages:
The first rhetorical detail is the pair of prepositions in verse 1, apo and dia: 'not from men nor through man.' Paul denies two sources. The first preposition denies a human origin, that is, that he got his office from any group of people. The second denies a human channel, that is, that someone appointed him by passing it down. He then gives one positive source with a single preposition governing both names, 'through Jesus Christ and God the Father.' The Father and the Son are linked under one preposition, which is a quiet statement of their unity.

The verb of rescue in verse 4 is exaireo, in the middle voice, which has the sense of snatching out for oneself. The aorist subjunctive after hopos gives the purpose: Christ gave Himself so that He might pluck us out. The verb is the one used in the Greek Old Testament for God delivering from Egypt and from enemies, and it is the same verb Paul's Lord uses for rescuing him from his own people in Acts 26:17. The phrase 'the present evil age' uses a perfect participle, enestotos, which means 'having stood in and now standing.' The age has not yet passed, but its grip has been broken for those who are in Christ. This is a short statement of the doctrine of the two ages.

In verse 6 the verb translated 'deserting' is metatithesthe. It means to move something from one place to another,, and in this setting it describes a change of allegiance. Paul's tense matters: it is present and the form can be middle or passive, so the Galatians are in the act of transferring their allegiance and the sentence calls them to stop. The adverb that goes with it, 'so quickly,' sharpens the alarm.

Paul then uses two Greek words for 'other.' The gospel they are turning to is heteron, another of a different kind, but he immediately says it is not allo, another of the same kind. There is no second gospel in the same sense. There is only the one, and counterfeits.

Verse 7 says some are 'distorting' the gospel, from metastrepho, to turn around or reverse. The false teachers do not delete the gospel but turn it inside out, until a message of free grace becomes a system of earned membership.

In verse 10 Paul asks whether he is now 'seeking the approval' of men, using the verb peitho, which has the sense of persuading or winning over. It can describe a speaker pleasing a crowd. The same verse calls him a 'servant' of Christ, using doulos, the word for a slave, and the contrast is deliberate: a slave of Christ cannot also be a slave to the opinions of others.

typology.fulfillment: God promised to bring Israel out from under the burdens of Egypt, and verse 4 uses language of rescue that sounds like the exodus on a larger scale. The pattern is fulfilled in Christ, who delivers not from a pharaoh but from the present evil age, and redeems at the cost of Himself, Titus 2:14. The type falls short because Israel was brought out of one place into another, while the new exodus changes the people and gives them a new age.

typology.type: The devoted thing under ban, Joshua 6:17-18
typology.fulfillment: The Hebrew idea of something set apart for destruction lies behind anathema. At Jericho, taking what was devoted brought the camp under the ban. Paul takes the idea to the gospel itself: to take a different one under one's roof brings the community under the same danger. Christ, in the greater fulfilment, becomes a curse for us, Galatians 3:13, so that the ban falls on Him. The type falls short because the ban at Jericho was about land and spoil, while here it concerns the truth of salvation.

typology.type: The true prophet and the false, Deuteronomy 13:1-5
typology.fulfillment: Moses told Israel that a prophet who did a sign yet led them toward other gods was to be refused, because the Lord was testing their love. Paul's 'even an angel from heaven' extends the test: the messenger's credentials do not decide it, the content does. In Christ the test is complete, for the Father speaks in the Son, Hebrews 1:1-2. The type falls short because it focused on gods other than the Lord, while here the deviation is subtle, a different gospel in the name of the same Lord.

study.christ:
The letter begins and ends with Christ, and these ten verses are already shaped by Him. The first thing to notice is the order of the names in verse 1. Paul is sent 'by Jesus Christ and God the Father,' with the Son named first and joined to the Father under one preposition. A man who writes this way cannot think of Jesus as merely a teacher. The one who sends is the one who raised Him, and the Son shares in the sending.

Next is the gospel in a sentence, verse 4. Christ 'gave Himself' for our sins. The verb has a sacrificial colour, and it gets repeated in 2:20, 'who loved me and gave Himself up for me.' The Gospels say the same: the Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The giving was voluntary, personal and substitutionary, 'for our sins,' and its purpose was rescue from the present evil age. Paul does not say Christ gave a teaching or an example, though He did both. He says He gave Himself.

The passage also shows what the gospel is not. If Christ gave Himself to rescue, then nothing can be added to the rescue without suggesting that He did not finish it. Paul will say later that if righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing, Galatians 2:21. The 'different gospel' of verse 6 is therefore not a smaller error. It treats the cross as incomplete.

There is also the matter of authority. The phrase 'the grace of Christ' in verse 6 is where the call of God is found. Grace is the means by which God calls, and Christ is its source. In verse 7 the false teachers distort 'the gospel of Christ,' meaning the message that belongs to Him and about Him.

Finally there is a quiet hint of Christ's rule. Paul calls himself a servant of Christ in verse 10, and the word is used for someone owned. To have Christ as Lord is to be free of the demands of every rival master. That freedom is the theme of the letter, and it begins with the Lord who gave Himself.

We should not claim more than the text gives. These verses do not give the whole account of how the cross works, and the letter develops it later, particularly in 3:13 and 4:4-5. What they give is the claim that it is enough.
study.god:
The passage shows God as the one who sends, raises, calls and rescues, and in each of these He is the actor. Paul is sent by Him. Jesus was raised by Him. The Galatians were called by Him. The rescue was according to His will. Verse 4 even says that it was done 'according to the will of our God and Father,' which makes the cross the expression of the Father's purpose and not an accident of history or a reluctant rescue. The Father who is named first in the greeting is the source of the grace they received.

God is also the one who raises the dead. This is introduced almost in passing in verse 1, but it shapes the whole letter. The same power that brought Jesus from the grave is the power that gives life to the believer. It is the reason the gospel is not a code to be kept but a work of God to be received.

The doxology of verse 5 tells us what God is owed. Glory belongs to Him forever, and the rescue was meant to bring it. Paul cannot hear the story of salvation without giving praise. This is the pattern of the Bible, in which God's saving acts end in worship, and it is the reason the letter's thanksgiving is replaced by a doxology.

God is jealous for His gospel, in the sense of being unwilling to share its credit. The curse on those who change it shows that He cares about the truth of the message and not only the sincerity of the messenger. Isaiah heard the Lord say, 'I will not yield My glory to another,' Isaiah 42:8. A gospel that rests partly on human achievement gives some of the glory to the achiever.

He is also the God who knows hearts. The question of verse 10, whether Paul is seeking the approval of God or of men, assumes that God's verdict is the one that counts, and Paul lives before it, as he says elsewhere, 'God, who examines our hearts,' 1 Thessalonians 2:4.

For worship and for life, the passage means that the believer rests in a work that God has finished, and gives glory for it, rather than working for acceptance. The right response to the gospel is Amen, and the right defence of it is the love that cannot see it abandoned.

crossReferences.note: Paul's opening to the Romans also joins his apostleship to the gospel of God, concerning His Son, declared with power by the resurrection. Set beside Galatians 1:1-5, it shows that the resurrection and the sending are tied together in the way he introduces himself.

The summary of the gospel Paul received and passed on: Christ died for our sins, was buried and was raised. It matches the shape of Galatians 1:1-4, with 'for our sins' and 'raised', and it shows the message was fixed and shared, not private.

Paul fears that the Corinthians, like Eve, will be led astray to another Jesus and a different gospel, and notes that they put up with it too easily. It is the same danger in the same words as Galatians 1:6-9.

False apostles disguise themselves as servants of righteousness, just as Satan does as an angel of light. This explains verse 8: an impressive messenger, even angelic in appearance, is not proof of a true message.
Moses sets the test for a prophet who works signs but leads away from the Lord: do not listen, because the Lord is testing love. Paul applies the same principle, that the message tests the messenger.
Israel is told not to add to or subtract from the commands of God. Paul's concern with a gospel that has been supplemented has behind it this long conviction that God's word is complete.

Men came down from Judea teaching that unless the brothers were circumcised they could not be saved. This is the historical shape of the problem Paul describes in Galatians, and it shows the issue was live across the churches.
Christ gave Himself for us to redeem us and make a people for Himself. The parallel with Galatians 1:4 shows the same verb of giving and the same purpose of rescue, now with the result named.
Paul would himself be cursed for the sake of his people. It guards against reading Galatians 1:8-9 as spite and shows the curse comes from a man who loves those he is warning.
Another use of anathema, here against anyone who does not love the Lord. It shows the word was part of Paul's vocabulary of final seriousness and that the gospel is bound to love for Christ.
Paul says he speaks as one approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, to please God and not men. It is the same defence as Galatians 1:10, from a gentler letter.

God has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His Son. It spells out the 'rescue' of Galatians 1:4 by naming the two realms between which the transfer takes place.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture begins with a good creation and a human race that turned from God. Everything that follows is the effect of that turning and God's answer to it. Galatians 1:4 names the situation in four words, 'the present evil age,' and offers the answer in a single clause: Christ gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from it. The whole biblical narrative is gathered up in that sentence, and Paul places it before he says anything else.

Looking back, the verse answers a long line of promises. God told Abraham that all nations would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3. The law and the prophets pointed to a rescue greater than the exodus. The sacrifices spoke of a life given for sin. Now the one who fulfils all of these has acted, and the rescue is complete. That is why Paul can describe the church as the people who live between the two ages, already rescued from the present evil age, though still living in it.

Looking forward, the rest of Galatians will show what this rescue means. The Galatians are not to be brought back under the law as a way to enter God's family. The curse of the law has been borne, 3:13. The adoption of sons and the gift of the Spirit have been given, 4:4-6. And a new creation has begun, 6:15. The letter keeps asking whether the final age has begun, and answers that it has, in Christ.

The warning against another gospel is also part of the larger story. Since the garden, the serpent has worked by altering what God has said. Paul links the two himself when he fears that minds will be led astray as Eve was by the serpent's cunning, 2 Corinthians 11:3. A changed gospel is the oldest strategy, dressed in the language of religion, and the church has to be on guard for it in every generation.

The story ends in the new creation, where there is no curse and God's people see His face, Revelation 22:3-4. The doxology of verse 5, 'to whom be glory forever and ever,' anticipates that ending. The people rescued from the present evil age are the same ones who will give glory to God for ever.

sermon.title: No Other Gospel (Galatians 1:3 to 12)
sermon.why: Keller works through Paul's alarm at the opening of Galatians, showing how Paul tests whether the true gospel is present by its power, content, drama, and intimacy, and why any addition to it is no gospel at all.

quiz.q: How does Paul summarize the gospel in verse 4?

options.text: Christ gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age.
options.note: The gospel is Christ's substitutionary self giving to deliver us.

options.text: Christ set us a good example to follow so we can save ourselves.
options.note: Christ is an example, but the verse stresses His self giving for our sins, not our self rescue.

options.text: Christ came only to teach us the law more clearly.
options.note: The point is rescue by His death, not clearer law teaching.

options.text: Christ leaves our salvation entirely up to our own effort.
options.note: He gave Himself for our sins; salvation is His work, not ours.

quiz.q: Why is Paul amazed at the Galatians?

options.text: They are so quickly deserting the God who called them and turning to a different gospel.
options.note: Verse 6 names their desertion of grace for a counterfeit.

options.text: They are simply asking a few honest questions about doctrine.
options.note: It is more than questions; they are turning away to another message.

options.text: They have stopped attending church altogether.
options.note: The issue is the content of the gospel, not mere attendance.

options.text: They are persecuting Paul personally.
options.note: The alarm is over the gospel being distorted, not personal attacks here.

quiz.q: What does Paul say about anyone who preaches a contrary gospel?

options.text: Let him be under a curse, even if it were Paul himself or an angel from heaven.
options.note: The double curse shows the gospel's content is not negotiable.

options.text: He should be gently ignored and left alone.
options.note: Paul does not ignore it; he pronounces a solemn curse.

options.text: He may be right if he is sincere.
options.note: Sincerity cannot rescue a false gospel; the message itself is condemned.

options.text: He should be welcomed as offering a helpful alternative.
options.note: There is no acceptable alternative to the one true gospel.

quiz.q: Where does Paul say his apostleship and gospel come from?

options.text: From Jesus Christ and God the Father, not from men.
options.note: Verse 1 grounds his authority in God, not human appointment.

options.text: From the other apostles who trained and sent him.
options.note: Paul stresses the opposite; his call came directly from God.

options.text: From his own study and reasoning.
options.note: He insists it was not devised by man but given by God.

options.text: From the approval of the crowds.
options.note: Verse 10 shows he does not live for human approval.

quiz.q: What does verse 10 reveal about Paul's motive?

options.text: He seeks to please God, not to win the approval of men.
options.note: A servant of Christ cannot live for human applause.

options.text: He wants to keep everyone comfortable and happy.
options.note: He explicitly refuses to make pleasing people his aim.

options.text: He is indifferent to what God thinks.
options.note: The opposite is true; God's approval is what he seeks.

options.text: He preaches whatever will grow the crowd fastest.
options.note: He would rather be cursed than distort the gospel for popularity.

questions: Paul defines the gospel as Christ giving Himself for our sins to rescue us. In your own words, what is the gospel, and does your answer put the weight on what Christ did or on what you do?
The Galatians drifted quickly from grace toward rule keeping. Where do you notice yourself adding conditions to God's acceptance, as if Christ were not quite enough?
Paul was willing to be cursed rather than change the message. What would it look like for you to love people enough to hold the truth of the gospel firmly?
Verse 10 asks whether we live for the approval of people or of God. Whose approval most drives your decisions this week?
The gospel rescues us from the present evil age. What in your life still feels like slavery, and how does Christ's self giving speak to it?

translationNotes.note: Under a curse translates anathema, devoted to destruction; the term is a solemn declaration of God's judgment, not a casual insult.
